extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology/criminology/cultural studies; policymakers and researchers interested in crime, moral panics and ideology
extracted.subtask_description: Reconstructing the deep-structure of traditionalist views and how social changes produce social anxiety, scapegoating, moral indignation and moral panics in public responses to crime (e.g., 'mugging'). Emphasis on class formations, media/judicial uses of lay vocabularies of motive, and the production of 'folk devils'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant ideas / hegemony
rubrics_metrics.description: "Dominant ideas are more inclusive in range: they encompass a wider slice of reality; they explain and reference things which take place on a larger plane, outside of 'immediate experience'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dominant ideas give exceptions and qualifications (contextualised judgments) a subordinate status, represent minority practices as universal, and are continually reproduced by ideological work. They conceal structured differences between classes, are foundational to cross-class alliances, and are given the form of universality as the only 'rational, universally valid' ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate / contextualised judgements as exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The contextualised judgements, the 'exceptions' to the general rule, do not often spawn counter-ideologies capable of challenging the over-all hegemony of 'ruling ideas'...The content of material social experience which informs subordinate value systems is, in fact, very different from that which is expressed in 'ruling ideas'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such judgments are situationally bound and so are treated as mere exceptions or qualifications within the dominant framework rather than as bases for alternative, universal ideologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universalising as 'common sense'
rubrics_metrics.description: "This structure of ruling ideas comes to be equated simply with 'how things are' and thus with 'common sense' itself - the one structure of ideas which everybody shares."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The universalising of 'common sense' masks class differences and produces the myth of a single national ethos (e.g., an English way of thought). This process sustains hegemony by presenting particular (often minority) practices as universally valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social anxiety (definition and origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Social anxiety - a product of both the dissolution of the material supports of that ideology, and the weakening of the broad social commitment to that ideology itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social anxiety arises when specific social changes undermine the material and ideological supports of traditionalist images (work, discipline, family). It predisposes sections of the population toward scapegoating and moral panic when they lack alternative ideological structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scapegoating (mechanism and production)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The emergence of a predisposition to the use of 'scapegoats', into which all the disturbing experiences are condensed and then symbolically rejected or 'cast out'...These scapegoats...are produced from specific conditions, by specific agencies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scapegoats condense diverse social dislocations (housing, family, law and order) and are not spontaneous: they are constructed and mobilised through ideological work (media, moral entrepreneurs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Break 1: Affluence → permissiveness (source of anxiety)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first had to do with 'affluence'...The association of 'affluence' with an attitude of 'unbridled materialism', hedonism and pleasure was seen as quickly leading on to 'permissiveness' - a state of the loosening of moral discipline, restraint and control."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affluence is experienced as moral erosion by groups invested in Protestant virtues (thrift, respectability). The perceived shift toward hedonism and permissiveness feeds moral indignation and anxiety among those who see their values undermined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break 2: Erosion of traditional working-class community
rubrics_metrics.description: "Urban redevelopment, changes in the local economies, in the structure of skills and occupations, increased geographical and educational mobility...had a combined and decomposing effect...on the respectable working-class community."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of neighbourhood ties, communal spaces, and informal social controls produces a sense of loss and unsettledness among middle-aged/older people, contributing to social anxiety and the search for symbolic targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folk Devil (concept and characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Folk Devil - on to whom all our most intense feelings about things going wrong...are projected - is...the reverse image, the alternative to all we know: the negation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A folk devil personifies collective fears and anxieties. Example: the 'mugger' — imagined as young, black, urban, motivated by gain, anatomising permissiveness and collapse of discipline. Folk devils crystallise otherwise diffuse discontents and catalyse moral panic and punitive demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral entrepreneurs / petty-bourgeois voice
rubrics_metrics.description: "The 'appeal to common sense', to the 'experience of the majority'...voiced by certain middle-class and, especially, lower-middle-class - or 'petty-bourgeois' social groups...They are the spear-head of the moral backlash...the moral entrepreneurs, the crusaders."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These groups mobilise moral indignation, claim to speak for the 'silent majority', write to local press, and use media forums to weld working-class and petty-bourgeois traditionalisms into a publicly resonant conservative coalition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'Englishness' thematic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Its ability to use that thematic structure of 'Englishness'...to connect with and draw out the otherwise unarticulated anxieties and sense of unease of those sections of the working class..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Themes like work, discipline and family (images of 'Englishness') are potent connectors that mobilise broad affective support for traditionalist coalitions even without detailed policy content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media/judicial reliance on fragmentary lay explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: "When the journalist, or the judge, or the members of the ordinary public have to respond to, or explain, troubling events...they tend to draw, often in a piecemeal and unreflexive manner, on the social images, the 'ideas of society'...which frame their everyday experience."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists, judges and the public employ incoherent, scattered vocabularies of motive rather than formal criminological theory; these lay explanations have practical explanatory power in news, legal reasoning and public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lay (fragmentary) vs. theorised criminological explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: "We are not here discussing fully coherent and adequately theorised explanations of crime...the more fragmentary, more incoherent and contradictory kinds of explanations which have explanatory power at the level of judicial reasoning, news and feature presentations...do indeed relate to the more elaborate 'criminological theories'..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the distinction: academic theories are systematic; public/journalistic explanations are piecemeal but influential. Analysts should trace relations between fragmentary public vocabularies and formal theories rather than dismissing the former as merely ignorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic condensation of diverse changes into composite images
rubrics_metrics.description: "What were in fact related but distinct developments were collapsed into three composite and overlapping images of unsettledness: youth, affluence and permissiveness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural dislocation tends to be symbolically focused on a small set of images (e.g., youth subcultures). These composite images simplify complex processes and make them available as targets for moral discourse and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggering and mobilisation of moral panics
rubrics_metrics.description: "Moral panics come into play when this deep-structure of anxiety and traditionalism connects with the public definition of crime by the media, and is mobilised."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When media definitions of crime link with pre-existing social anxiety and traditionalist imagery, they can mobilise disproportionate moral indignation, produce folk devils, and legitimize calls for punitive control beyond the scale of the actual threat.
